name: Montepulciano

lines.s10: Montepulciano is the dark, generous red of Abruzzo: black cherry and plum, soft acidity and plenty of round tannin.
lines.s20: Montepulciano is the red grape of Italy's Adriatic side, above all in Abruzzo, where it makes Montepulciano d'Abruzzo. It is deep purple and plummy, with black cherry, soft acidity and a round, generous grip.
lines.s45: Montepulciano grows down the Adriatic side of Italy, and Abruzzo is its heart. It ripens late, into October, and gives a deep purple wine of black cherry and plum. The acidity is soft and the tannin plentiful but round. Most is fermented quickly and bottled young, while a few hill estates age it for years in large casks. Pressed off its skins after a few hours, it also makes Cerasuolo, a cherry red rosé. It belongs with skewers of grilled lamb, sausages or pasta in a meat sauce. Do not confuse it with Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, the Tuscan town's wine, which is Sangiovese.
lines.sale: Montepulciano is a grape, not the Tuscan town, and in Abruzzo it makes a dark, round red full of black cherry. I would pour it with the lamb or the sausage pasta, or begin with a glass of its cherry red rosé.

glass.lead: Black cherry and black plum in a deep purple glass, with soft acidity and plentiful, ripe, round tannin.

ladder.where: The Peligna valley and the Ofena plateau, high in the Apennines
The Chieti hills near the Adriatic, and Australia's Barossa

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity low to medium, tannin medium to medium plus, ripe and round, alcohol medium plus, body medium plus to full; deep purple.

home.home: Abruzzo is its heartland: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, at least 85 per cent of the grape, the Colline Teramane DOCG in the Teramo hills, and Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo, its cherry red rosé. The Marche makes Conero from it and blends it into Rosso Piceno.
home.abroad: Molise, Puglia and the Roma DOC grow it too. Beyond Italy it is a newcomer: Australia has planted it in warm regions such as the Barossa and the Riverland, where it ripens late and fully.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; a Colline Teramane Riserva a little warmer.
service.glass: A Bordeaux glass, with room for the dark fruit and ripe tannin.
service.decant: Rarely for an everyday bottle; consider it for a young Colline Teramane Riserva after a taste.
service.age: Most within three to five years; Colline Teramane and the slow, traditional estates ten or more.

with.why: dark fruit and gentle acidity suit a rich sauce

firmer tannin for a slow cooked roast

labels.means: At least 85 per cent Montepulciano from Abruzzo; Riserva ages at least two years.
The DOCG of the Teramo hills, at least 90 per cent Montepulciano; Riserva three years, one in wood.
The deep cherry red rosé of Montepulciano, its own DOC since 2010; cerasa means cherry.
The Marche's Montepulciano reds: Conero from the headland above Ancona, Rosso Piceno blended with Sangiovese.
Sangiovese from the Tuscan town of that name, not this grape.

guest.q: Is this the same as Vino Nobile di Montepulciano?
guest.a: No. Vino Nobile is Sangiovese from the Tuscan town of Montepulciano. This is the Montepulciano grape, grown down the Adriatic side and in Abruzzo above all.
The rosé of Montepulciano in Abruzzo, named for the cherry. It is pressed off the skins after a few hours, so it is darker than most pinks, dry, with real grip.

guest.q: Will it be a heavy wine?
guest.a: Deep in colour and generous, but rarely hard: the acidity is soft and the tannin round, so it drinks easily young.

compare.tell: Sangiovese is paler and tarter, with tomato leaf and a dusty grip; Montepulciano is deeper in colour, with black cherry and plum and softer acidity.
Aglianico is firmer and more acidic, with high, drying tannin and a smoky edge; Montepulciano is rounder, softer in acidity and readier young.

profile.st: Deep purple ruby · Body medium plus to full · Acid low to medium · Tannin medium to medium plus, ripe and round · Alcohol medium plus · Dry
profile.fruit: Black cherry, black plum, blackberry; sour cherry and wild strawberry in the Cerasuolo rosé
profile.other: Liquorice, black pepper and leather, with a touch of dried leaves; vanilla and cocoa where new barrels are used
profile.tell: Deep purple with ripe black cherry and plum, plentiful but round tannin and soft acidity: dark and generous, rarely sharp
profile.regions: Abruzzo (Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, Colline Teramane, Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo), the Marche (Conero, Rosso Piceno), Molise, Puglia, Lazio
profile.confuse: Sangiovese is paler and tarter, with tomato leaf; Aglianico is firmer and more acidic; Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese, not this grape

cards.front: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano: which grape is in each?
cards.back: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is the Montepulciano grape. Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese, named for a Tuscan town.

cards.front: Montepulciano: what is Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo, and how is it made?
cards.back: Its deep cherry red rosé, a DOC since 2010. The grapes are pressed off their skins after a few hours, so it keeps colour and real tannin.

cards.front: Montepulciano: the Abruzzo DOCG of the Teramo hills, and its rules?
cards.back: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo Colline Teramane: at least 90 per cent Montepulciano, firmer than the plain DOC; Riserva three years, at least one in wood.

questions.q: An Italian red poured blind is deep purple, with ripe black cherry and plum, soft acidity and plentiful but round tannin. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Deep colour, ripe black cherry and plum, soft acidity and round tannin are Montepulciano. Sangiovese, the nearest wrong option, would be paler and tarter, with tomato leaf and dusty tannin.

questions.q: A guest asks for a Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and the server brings a Vino Nobile di Montepulciano. What has gone wrong?
opts: Vino Nobile is Sangiovese from a Tuscan town
Vino Nobile is the Riserva of the same wine
Vino Nobile is the rosé of the same grape
Vino Nobile is Montepulciano from the Marche
questions.exp: Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is named for the grape; Vino Nobile is named for the Tuscan town and made mainly from Sangiovese. The rosé of the Montepulciano grape is Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo.

questions.q: A guest wants an Italian rosé dark and firm enough for grilled meat. Of these four on the list, which do you pour?
questions.exp: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is Montepulciano pressed after a few hours on its skins: cherry red, dry and gripping. Cerasuolo di Vittoria, the nearest miss, shares the word but is a Sicilian red.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it. A new grape: the profile is written new and the targets are the four regions the Codex already joins to the name (abruzzo, marche, lazio, italy) and puglia, whose record names Montepulciano at San Severo and beside Nero di Troia.

The Abruzzo facts (almost the whole red vineyard, at least 85 per cent in the DOC, Colline Teramane at 90 per cent with a three year Riserva, Cerasuolo its own DOC since 2010 and pressed after hours on the skins, late ripening into October, quick warm fermentation and young bottling beside a slow school of large casks, the Peligna valley and Ofena for freshness), the Marche's Conero and Rosso Piceno, Molise's Biferno, the Roma DOC at half Montepulciano and the Vino Nobile trap all stand on the Codex's Abruzzo, Marche, Lazio, Puglia and Italy records. The 85 per cent rule also stands on the region's own regulation.

The Codex's Abruzzo and Marche records describe the tannin differently (soft tannin in Abruzzo, firm, ripe tannin in the Marche); the entry says plentiful but round, medium to medium plus, which both fit.

notIn: the brief's example for this grape was vino nobile, vino nobile di montepulciano and rosso di montepulciano, but vino nobile would shut out the Régionale question on telling Montepulciano d'Abruzzo from Vino Nobile, which belongs in this drill. Tested against the four level banks through the chain: the montepulciano key gathers eleven bank questions; prugnolo gentile shuts out the five that are Sangiovese's (the Chianti, Montalcino and Montepulciano question, the hill town question, the Biondi Santi question, the Vino Nobile seventy per cent question and the Advanced local name question), vin santo shuts out the Master Vin Santo question that names Vin Santo di Montepulciano, and rosso di montepulciano guards the Court's pair. The five that stay are the grape's own: the grape and town question, both Cerasuolo questions, Rosso Conero and Colline Teramane.

Abroad: Australia's plantings in warm regions such as the Barossa and the Riverland, late ripening and unsuited to cool sites, stand on the Australian Wine Research Institute and the Wine and Viticulture Journal; the sites were read through search results only.
The Creole dish is crawfish étouffée with Cerasuolo, a dark, dry rosé with grip; the Codex's Abruzzo record pairs Cerasuolo with fish stews and grilled meat.
The named notes cracked black pepper, dried leaves and cocoa are a taster's naming beside the Codex's touch of earth; a checker should weigh them.

checked.verdict: Sound after three fixes. The rules, the rosé, the notIn list and the targets stand; the home line gave a share of plantings and the blind question named Abruzzo in its stem.
changed: worlds.home.home: Almost the whole red vineyard is a share of plantings, which the house rules keep out as volatile, though the Codex's Abruzzo record says it. Heartland says where it belongs without a share.

questions.0.q: The stem showed a label from Abruzzo, which gives the key away. The glass alone, on an Italian list, now carries it, and each other grape fails a cue: Sangiovese and Aglianico the soft acidity, Nebbiolo the deep colour.
questions.0.exp: From Abruzzo leaves the explanation with the stem.
open: The Codex's Abruzzo record calls the grape one of the most planted reds of Italy and almost the whole of the region's red vineyard: a volatile planting claim in a reviewed record, left for the owner.
